results.message: Was Augustine's account of Pelagius fair?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
We do not know whether Augustine gave Pelagius's own teaching fairly. What Augustine answered across thirteen works is real and documented - that was his own long fight. But whether Pelagius himself held the claim Augustine answered is contested, not settled. The claim Augustine sets out is this: a believer's own moral effort, unaided, is enough to obey what God commands. Whether that was Pelagius's own view, stated that way, we cannot say from our own evidence. What we can say is that the argument itself runs deep in our later years, not across our whole span. The theme touches Cyprian only in passing. A heading in Cyprian's handbook of proof texts says we must boast in nothing, since nothing is our own: “We must boast in nothing, since nothing is our own. The Gospel according to John says, “No one can receive anything unless it is given to him from heaven.” Paul's first letter to the Corinthians also says, “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?””

Augustine quoted those very words against the Pelagians. But in Cyprian's time, nothing was organized around it. In Augustine's own years it shaped formation heavily. The corpus that carries the argument is the largest single body of text we have, and it is Augustine's alone.

citations.sentence: But whether Pelagius himself held the claim Augustine answered is contested, not settled.

sources.label: Augustine's own anti-Pelagian corpus accurately represents the position Pelagius himself held -- that a believer's own moral effort, unaided, is sufficient to obey what God commands -- and the later Reformation-era and modern Catholic/Protestant use of this same controversy to stake out opposing positions on grace and merit continues an argument whose terms Augustine himself correctly set.

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV, independently re-located this session; Doc_01 SS2); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII; Doc_01 SS2); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo (lpc.story.the-psalms-on-the-wall)

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised (Doc_01 SS2; lpc.story.election-of-cyprian); banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258 (lpc.story.the-death-of-cyprian)
